title: Pinchas: a shepherd for the flock (Numbers 27:15–17)
hook: Moses asks for a successor so the people won't be sheep without a shepherd

segments.voice: Yesterday, five sisters stood at the Tent of Meeting and asked to inherit, and God said the daughters speak right. Your line was the daughters speak right. Did you make a fair request out loud? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

A doctor's office, and the news no one wants to hear. How long? What can I do? Is there anything else? Those would be fair first questions. Right after the five sisters' case, God tells Moses to climb a mountain and look out at the land he will not enter, because soon he will die, like Aaron. It's hard news after so many years of leading. And the first words out of his mouth aren't about himself at all.
screen: `THE NEWS NO ONE WANTS.` → `CLIMB THE MOUNTAIN AND LOOK.` → `HIS FIRST WORDS AREN'T ABOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Moses answers, in paraphrase: let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint someone over the community, someone who will go out before them and come in before them, who will lead them out and bring them in, and then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd." No protest. No bargaining for more time, not here. His first worry is the people after him. Look at the name he uses for God: the God of the spirits of all flesh. Rashi hears a request inside it. You know, Moses is saying, that every person's mind is different. Give them a leader who can bear with each one of them as they are. Moses had spent his years of leading learning exactly that. And notice the picture of a leader he asks for: one who goes out before them and comes in before them. Not one who sends people ahead, but one who walks first. Moses had been a shepherd before he was a prophet; he'd tended his father-in-law's flock in the wilderness when God first called him. He knew what happens to sheep with nobody in front. The midrash adds a human touch. It says Moses may have hoped one of his own sons would take over. Instead God chose Joshua, who had served Moses faithfully, and stayed close to the tent, for years. Moses didn't argue. The question he asked, before anything about himself, is one that parents, teachers and founders come to face too: who comes next?
screen: `HIS FIRST WORRY: THE PEOPLE AFTER HIM.` · `GOD OF THE SPIRITS OF ALL FLESH.` · `ONE WHO GOES OUT BEFORE THEM.` · `NOT HIS SONS, BUT JOSHUA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare someone to follow you. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you do that matters to others: a job, a family role, a skill, a group you hold together. If you stepped away tomorrow, who would carry it? Picture that person. What's one thing you know that they don't yet? A recipe, where the spare key is kept, a way of handling a hard customer, a family story. Decide on one thing you could teach or write down for them this week. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pinchas. The portion where Moses, told he will die, first asks for a shepherd so the people won't be sheep without one.
Your line: who comes next. Today, teach one small thing you know to someone who might need it after you. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

screen: `DAY 468 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PINCHAS: SOME OF THY HONOR.`

howItsDone: Moses' request for a successor is read in the portion of Pinchas in summer, and the phrase 'sheep without a shepherd' is often quoted in Jewish teaching about leadership and responsibility.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've just learned you won't enter the land and will soon die. what do you say first?
options: appoint someone, so they won't be sheep without a shepherd.
let my sons lead after me.
fork.reveal: his first words are for the people: let God appoint a leader, so the congregation won't be as sheep which have no shepherd.

original.note: Hebrew: God of the spirits of all flesh, the name Moses uses as he asks for a successor (Numbers 27:16).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old leader picks a replacement.
what it means: told he will die, Moses' first concern is that the people have a shepherd who walks in front of them.
what a scholar hears: Rashi reads 'God of the spirits of all flesh' as a plea for a leader who can bear each person's different temperament; the midrash says Moses hoped for his sons.

sources.quoted: that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd.

notes: Numbers 27:17 JPS 1917: confirm wording ('that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd').
Rashi on 27:16: each person's temperament differs; appoint a leader who can bear with each. Confirm.
Midrash that Moses hoped his sons would succeed him (Rashi on 27:16 citing Tanchuma; Bamidbar Rabbah 21:14); confirm references.
The hook says Moses doesn't bargain 'here'; in Deuteronomy 3:23–26 he does plead to enter the land. The script's 'not here' is meant to leave room for that.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens with 'Imagine' or claims 'most of us'; cut 'the hardest news of his life' and both 'forty years' figures (not in Numbers 27); softened 'every parent, teacher and founder'.
